news-snowman-prize-6.text: Keep laundry, curtains, and bedding well away from space heaters, and never leave one running while you sleep.

news-snowman-prize-7.text: Officials also suggest checking that your smoke alarm works by pressing its test button.

news-snowman-prize-8.text: And if you use a gas or kerosene heater, open a window from time to time.

news-soup-week-1.text: Good morning, and welcome to the island news. I'm Isabelle.

news-soup-week-2.text: First up, the café is serving a different winter soup each day this week, made with vegetables from the community garden.

news-soup-week-3.text: A bowl costs four hundred yen, though residents who bring their own mug pay just three hundred.

news-soup-week-4.text: Proceeds will go toward new books for the library.

news-soup-week-5.text: Turning to the city, Tokyo health officials are warning about sudden temperature changes in the bathroom during winter.

news-star-night-1.text: Good morning, everyone. Here's a look at what's happening on the island.

news-star-night-2.text: First up, the island's summer stargazing night is slated for later this week on the hilltop by the museum.

news-star-night-3.text: Our resident stargazer will lead the event, which now begins at nine-fifteen rather than eight-forty-five, once the sky is fully dark.

news-star-night-4.text: Telescopes will be shared, but organizers suggest bringing a blanket and insect spray.

news-star-night-5.text: Turning to the city, summer in Tokyo is festival season, and neighborhood events can draw big crowds.

news-star-night-6.text: Organizers are asking visitors to carry their trash home, since temporary bins tend to overflow by evening.

news-star-night-7.text: Police also remind people to follow staff directions near stations, where crowds can build up quickly after the events end.

news-star-night-8.text: If you're wearing a yukata, give yourself extra time to get there.

news-story-hour-1.text: Good morning, island. Isabelle here with today's top stories.

news-story-hour-2.text: First up, the library is starting a weekly story hour for young residents, held in the reading room upstairs.

news-story-hour-3.text: Each session runs forty minutes, not fourteen as printed on the flyer, and no sign-up is needed.

news-story-hour-4.text: The librarian is also asking for donations of picture books in good condition.

news-story-hour-5.text: Turning to the city, spring weekends bring big crowds to Tokyo's parks for picnics under the trees.

news-story-hour-6.text: Park officials are reminding visitors to take their trash home, since bins fill up quickly on busy days.

news-story-hour-7.text: They're also asking groups not to save large spaces with tarps early in the morning and then leave them empty.

news-story-hour-8.text: And many parks ban barbecues, so check the rules before you go.

news-wx-alert-fog.text: Dense fog could cut visibility early on, so drivers, please take extra care.

news-wx-alert-hot.text: It'll feel hot and sticky out there, so remember to stay hydrated.

news-wx-alert-snow.text: Roads and sidewalks could get slippery, so take it slow and leave a little extra time.

news-wx-alert-storm.text: A heavy rain advisory is in effect, so watch out for flooded streets and train delays.

news-wx-end.text: And that's the news for this morning. I'm Isabelle. Have a wonderful day!

serial-johnny-1-30.text: He sat on a low plastic stool and watched the crowd go by, couples and families and students, all of them in no hurry at all.

serial-johnny-1-31.text: Somewhere in all that happiness, he took his old brass compass out of his pocket to check the way back to the ship.

serial-johnny-1-32.text: And that, he said, was the very last time he ever saw it.

serial-johnny-1-33.text: Oh no, your compass? Is that how ya ended up here again?

serial-johnny-1-34.text: Well, one thing led to another, as they say. But that, my friends, is a story for tomorrow night.

serial-johnny-1-35.text: And with that, Gulliver pulled his cap down over his eyes and fell asleep before the fire burned down.

serial-johnny-1-36.text: Dom put a blanket over him. And the waves kept coming in, slow and steady, all night long.

serial-johnny-1-4.text: Whoa, whoa. Hey, buddy, you okay? You're kinda soaked, man.

serial-johnny-1-5.text: The laundry sat up, blinked at the sky, and fixed a sailor's cap that had seen much better days.

serial-johnny-1-6.text: Ah, good morning, sailor! Tell me, is this Hawaii? It feels a little bit like Hawaii.

serial-johnny-1-7.text: Nope, it's jus' our island. But hey, welcome back, Gulliver. This is, like, your fifth time.

serial-johnny-1-8.text: Gulliver did not remember the island. He never did, no matter how many times he washed up on it. But he remembered the coffee.

serial-johnny-1-9.text: By evening, word had gotten around. A small fire was crackling on the beach, and a few neighbors had come down with mugs of cocoa.

serial-johnny-2-1.text: The next night was cooler, and the fire was a little bigger. Maple had brought a thermos of hot cider, and Kicks had brought his own folding chair.

serial-johnny-2-10.text: The cabin was small and made of logs, with a wood stove in the middle that kept the whole place warm and smelling like pine.

serial-johnny-2-11.text: That night, it started to snow. Not the light, pretty kind. The serious kind, the kind that doesn't plan on stopping.

serial-johnny-2-12.text: By morning, the snow was halfway up the windows, and the power was out. They were snowed in, and the whole world was quiet and white.

serial-johnny-2-13.text: Oh my gosh, that sounds so cozy. Weren'tcha scared, though, bein' stuck out there?

serial-johnny-2-14.text: Not one bit. Ruth said, out here, you don't fight the snow. You just make more soup and wait it out.

serial-johnny-2-15.text: So that's what they did. They kept the stove going, played cards by candlelight, and told the same old sea stories they had told a hundred times.

serial-johnny-2-16.text: Ruth cheated at cards. Gulliver knew it, and Ruth knew he knew it, and neither of them said a word about it.

serial-johnny-2-17.text: On the second day, Ruth said she had a treat for him. She heated a pot of maple syrup on the stove until it was bubbling.

serial-johnny-2-18.text: Then she went outside, packed a pan full of clean, fresh snow, and poured the hot syrup over it in thin lines.

serial-johnny-2-19.text: It turns into this soft, chewy candy, right there on the snow. You pick it up with a fork. They call it sugar on snow.

serial-johnny-2-2.text: Okay, okay, so you lost the compass. Then what? Didja get on the wrong ship or somethin'?

serial-johnny-2-20.text: Wait, wait. Maple syrup on snow? Okay, I needa try that. Like, right now.

serial-johnny-2-21.text: And here's the strange part. She served it with a plain donut and a sour pickle on the side.

serial-johnny-2-22.text: A pickle? C'mon, man. You're makin' that up. Nobody eats a pickle with candy.

serial-johnny-2-23.text: I swear on my cap. The pickle cuts the sweetness, so you can keep eating. It's a Vermont thing. And it works.

serial-johnny-2-24.text: On the third day, they heard a low rumble through the trees.

serial-johnny-2-25.text: It was the snowplow, pushing a clean path down the road. And the power came back on.

serial-johnny-2-26.text: Gulliver was almost sad. He had gotten used to the quiet, and to losing at cards.

serial-johnny-2-27.text: Before he left, Ruth took a faded postcard out of an old wooden box.

serial-johnny-2-28.text: It showed a small white ferry on a calm blue sea, with green islands all around.

serial-johnny-2-29.text: She said, it's in Japan. The Seto Inland Sea. I always meant to go and never did. So you go, and tell me about it.

serial-johnny-2-3.text: How did you know? That's exactly what happened. I got on a big cargo ship, and a month later, I was in Boston.

serial-johnny-2-30.text: Gulliver put the postcard in his inside pocket, right where the compass used to be. And that's where he kept it, the whole way across the world.

serial-johnny-2-31.text: Dude, that's actually really sweet. Didja ever write to her?

serial-johnny-2-32.text: Not yet. I'm still working on it. But first, I have to tell you about the ferry. Tomorrow night.

serial-johnny-2-33.text: Maple poured the last of the cider. And somewhere far away, it was snowing on a little log cabin in the woods.

serial-johnny-2-4.text: Boston in March is not a place for a sailor in a thin jacket. The wind came off the harbor like it had something personal against him.

serial-johnny-2-5.text: So Gulliver did what any sensible bird would do. He bought a wool hat, a very large coffee, and a bus ticket north.

serial-johnny-2-6.text: I have an old shipmate in Vermont. Ruth. We sailed together for years, and then she retired to a cabin in the woods.

serial-johnny-2-7.text: The bus wound its way up into the hills. Little white churches, red barns, and snow on everything, like someone had covered the world in frosting.

serial-johnny-2-8.text: Ruth met him at the bus stop in an old pickup truck. She was wearing a red plaid coat and the same big grin he remembered.

serial-johnny-2-9.text: First thing she said was, you look terrible. Second thing she said was, get in, there's soup.

serial-johnny-3-1.text: On the third night, there was no wind at all. The sea was flat and silver under the moon, which, Gulliver said, was perfect for a ferry story.

serial-johnny-3-10.text: Inside, there was a room with a tatami floor, and people just lay down on it.

serial-johnny-3-11.text: Grandparents, students, a man in a suit with his shoes lined up neatly by the door.

serial-johnny-3-12.text: Wait, people jus' sleep on the floor? On the ferry? That's awesome. I'd be out in, like, two minutes.

serial-johnny-3-13.text: That's the thing. I meant to stay awake. I really did. I had my postcard out and everything.

serial-johnny-3-14.text: The islands slid past the windows, green and soft and round, with lemon trees growing in rows down the hillsides, right to the water.

serial-johnny-3-15.text: On one island, a giant yellow pumpkin with black polka dots sat at the end of a pier, like it was waiting for a boat too.

serial-johnny-3-16.text: A giant pumpkin? With polka dots? Okay, now I know you're jus' messin' with us.

serial-johnny-3-17.text: It's art! Famous art! People come from all over the world just to take a picture with it.

serial-johnny-3-18.text: At the next stop, an old fisherman got on with a bucket and sat down next to Gulliver.

serial-johnny-3-19.text: He didn't say much. He just smiled and handed him a mee-kahn.

serial-johnny-3-2.text: Cherry had come down with a bag of marshmallows to roast, and Dom was back, still in his running shorts, even though it was cold.

serial-johnny-3-20.text: Then another mee-kahn. Then a third. By the time they had passed two islands, Gulliver had a little pile of orange peels on his lap.

serial-johnny-3-21.text: We didn't share a language, him and me. But we shared a lot of fruit. I think that counts for something.

serial-johnny-3-22.text: And then, with the sun on the tatami and the engine humming under the floor, Gulliver lay down, just to rest his eyes for a moment.

serial-johnny-3-23.text: When he opened them again, the ferry was back where it started. He had missed his stop.

serial-johnny-3-24.text: Oh, man. That's rough. So what'dja do? Just get off an' try again tomorrow?

serial-johnny-3-25.text: Try again tomorrow? Nonsense. I stayed on and went right back the other way. And then I fell asleep again.

serial-johnny-3-26.text: He missed his stop three times that day. Back and forth, back and forth, across the same calm water.

serial-johnny-3-27.text: The ferry crew started to recognize him. On the last trip, one of them brought him a cup of green tea without being asked.

serial-johnny-3-28.text: Honestly, it was the best mistake I've ever made. I saw every island twice, and I've never slept better in my life.

serial-johnny-3-29.text: Okay, I'll admit it, that's kinda perfect. So didja ever get off the boat?

serial-johnny-3-3.text: So ya went to Japan, just 'cause of a postcard? Like, that's it? That's the whole reason?

serial-johnny-3-30.text: Eventually. At the very last port, as the sun went down, there was a big ship in the harbor with a sign. It said, Los Angeles.

serial-johnny-3-31.text: And Gulliver, who never could say no to a sign, picked up his bag and walked straight toward it.

serial-johnny-3-32.text: Dom was already yawning. Cherry ate the last marshmallow. And the moon sat on the flat, silver sea, as calm as a ferry with nowhere special to be.

serial-johnny-3-4.text: My dear, a postcard is the best reason there is. Most of my trips start with worse ones.

serial-johnny-3-5.text: He got a job on a ship heading for Japan, peeling potatoes in the kitchen. Six weeks of potatoes, he said. He still dreams about them.

serial-johnny-3-6.text: He got off in a little port town on the coast. The streets went steeply up the hill, and there were cats sleeping on almost every step.

serial-johnny-3-7.text: One of them followed me all the way to the ferry. Big orange fellow. I think he wanted my sandwich more than my company.

serial-johnny-3-8.text: The ferry was small and white, just like the one in the postcard. It wasn't fast. It wasn't fancy. It was in no rush to get anywhere.

serial-johnny-3-9.text: It went from island to island, stopping at tiny piers where a few people got off and a few people got on, and somebody always waved.

serial-johnny-4-1.text: On the fourth night, Bunnie came early with a basket of snacks, and Redd showed up late, claiming he just happened to be walking by.

serial-johnny-4-10.text: Ooh, I love those! The shiny ones, with the lil stools that spin around? Please tell me it had the stools.

serial-johnny-4-11.text: It had the stools. Red ones. I spun around on mine twice before Earl gave me a look.

serial-johnny-4-12.text: Behind the counter was a waitress named Darlene, with big hair and a pencil behind her ear. She called everybody hun. Earl, Gulliver, even the cook.

serial-johnny-4-13.text: She poured Gulliver a cup of coffee before he even sat down. And every time the cup got half empty, she came back and filled it up again.

serial-johnny-4-14.text: I asked her, how much for the refills? And she said, hun, it's bottomless. I almost cried. That's my favorite word in English.

serial-johnny-4-15.text: Bottomless, huh? Free refills? Now that's what I call a business model. I gotta get in on that.

serial-johnny-4-16.text: Earl ordered the meatloaf. Gulliver asked Darlene what was good, and she leaned in and said, the cherry pie, hun. Trust me.

serial-johnny-4-17.text: It came warm, with a scoop of vanilla ice cream melting slowly down the side. Pie à la mode, Darlene called it.

serial-johnny-4-18.text: I'll tell you something. I've had pepper buns in Taipei and sugar on snow in Vermont. That pie was right up there with them.

serial-johnny-4-19.text: In a booth, a family on a road trip was arguing about the Grand Canyon. The kids wanted to see it. The dad wanted a bed.

serial-johnny-4-2.text: Don't mind me, I'm jus' passin' through. Is that a story I hear? I love a good story. Especially a free one.

serial-johnny-4-20.text: Earl turned around on his stool and told them, it's just a big hole in the ground. But it's a big hole you've got to see.

serial-johnny-4-21.text: When it was time to pay, Gulliver counted out exactly what the check said. Earl shook his head and put a few more dollars on the counter.

serial-johnny-4-22.text: He said, in this country, you tip, son. Darlene's on her feet all night. So I tipped. Generously. With my last few dollars.

serial-johnny-4-23.text: Aw, that's so nice of ya. So then what? You just got back in the truck an' kept going?

serial-johnny-4-24.text: Then we stepped outside, and I looked up. I've been at sea my whole life, and I have never seen so many stars.

serial-johnny-4-25.text: There was no moon, and no city for a hundred miles. The sky was more stars than dark, and they could hear the neon sign humming.

serial-johnny-4-26.text: Then Darlene came out with a coffee to go, for the road. She asked where Gulliver was headed, and he said he honestly had no idea.

serial-johnny-4-27.text: And she said, well, hun, my brother keeps a lighthouse up in Maine, and he could use some help this winter. Interested?

serial-johnny-4-28.text: A lighthouse, huh? Lemme guess. Ya said yes before she even finished the sentence.

serial-johnny-4-29.text: I said yes before she finished the word lighthouse. But that, my friends, is tomorrow's story. The last one.

serial-johnny-4-3.text: Gulliver cleared his throat. The ship from Japan, he said, took him all the way across the Pacific to the port of Los Angeles.

serial-johnny-4-30.text: Bunnie packed up the basket. Redd took the leftover snacks, for safekeeping, he said. And above the island, there seemed to be more stars than usual.

serial-johnny-4-4.text: Los Angeles is a lovely place, but everyone's in a car. A sailor without a car is a sailor without legs.

serial-johnny-4-5.text: Lucky for him, a truck driver named Earl was having breakfast at the port. Earl was heading east with a load of watermelons and wanted some company.

serial-johnny-4-6.text: Earl didn't talk much. But when he did, it was worth waiting for. He said, the desert's got two speeds, son. Slow and slower.

serial-johnny-4-7.text: They drove for hours. The city turned into hills, and the hills turned into desert, with mountains far away that never got any closer.

serial-johnny-4-8.text: By the time the sun went down, they were on an old highway, the famous one, Route Sixty-Six. And up ahead, there was a light.

serial-johnny-4-9.text: It was a neon sign, pink and blue, buzzing a little, with three big letters that said EAT. Under it was a small silver diner.

serial-johnny-5-1.text: On the fifth night, more neighbors came than ever. Maple, Dom, and Goldie sat closest to the fire, with blankets over their knees.

serial-johnny-5-10.text: A hundred an' twelve stairs? Every day? Dude, that's a serious leg workout. I'm kinda jealous.

serial-johnny-5-11.text: On Sundays, Walt drove them into town for lobster rolls. Big pieces of lobster in a buttered, toasted bun, eaten on a bench by the harbor.

serial-johnny-5-12.text: Walt said, you don't eat a lobster roll inside. It's against the rules. So we sat outside and froze, and it was wonderful.

serial-johnny-5-13.text: Then one February night, the fog rolled in, so thick you couldn't see your own feet. And the old foghorn coughed once and went quiet.

serial-johnny-5-14.text: Walt listened to the radio and frowned. A small fishing boat was still out there. The captain couldn't find the harbor in the fog.

serial-johnny-5-15.text: Oh no. That's so scary. Couldn't they jus' follow the light from the lighthouse?

serial-johnny-5-16.text: That's what I thought, too. But in fog like that, the light just disappears. You can't see a thing. But you can still hear.

serial-johnny-5-17.text: There was an old brass bell on the rocks below the lighthouse, from the days before electric foghorns. Walt handed Gulliver the rope.

serial-johnny-5-18.text: Walt stayed on the radio, telling the captain to steer toward the sound. And Gulliver rang the bell. Slow and steady, again and again.

serial-johnny-5-19.text: I rang that bell for two hours. My arms were shaking. I sang every sea song I know, just to keep the rhythm.

serial-johnny-5-2.text: Okay, last one. I'm kinda sad, honestly. I've gotten used to this. Same time every night, y'know?

serial-johnny-5-20.text: And then, out of the white, they saw two small lights, red and green. The fishing boat came around the rocks and into the harbor, safe.

serial-johnny-5-21.text: The next morning, the captain came up the hill with a bag of fresh fish and a small wooden box. Inside the box was a brand new compass.

serial-johnny-5-22.text: He said, a sailor should always know the way home. And I almost cried for the second time on this trip. Bottomless coffee was the first.

serial-johnny-5-23.text: That night, he finally wrote to Ruth and told her all about the ferry.

serial-johnny-5-24.text: When spring came, Gulliver said goodbye to Walt and got on a ship heading south, with the new compass safe in his pocket.

serial-johnny-5-25.text: And then, of course, there was a storm. A big one. The kind sailors tell stories about.

serial-johnny-5-26.text: And the next thing he knew, Dom was standing over him on the beach.

serial-johnny-5-27.text: Wait a sec. So where's the new compass? The one from the fishin' captain?

serial-johnny-5-28.text: Gulliver patted his left pocket. Then his right pocket. Then the inside of his cap. He looked up at everyone with a very small smile.

serial-johnny-5-29.text: Well. It seems I've lost it again. But you know, I'm starting to think that's not such a bad thing.

serial-johnny-5-3.text: Me too, my dear. Me too. Now, where was I? Ah, yes. Maine.

serial-johnny-5-30.text: Everybody laughed, and the fire popped, and for a while nobody said anything. They just watched the sparks go up into the dark.

serial-johnny-5-31.text: In the morning, Gulliver was gone. There was only a long line of footprints going down to the water, and a message written in the sand.

serial-johnny-5-32.text: It said, thank you for the coffee. Back soon. Probably by accident.

serial-johnny-5-33.text: And the tide came in, slowly, and smoothed the sand, the way it always does. Goodnight.

serial-johnny-5-4.text: From the desert, he took a long train across the whole country. Four days of farms and rivers and little towns going by the window.

serial-johnny-5-5.text: At the end of it was a rocky coast, cold and gray and beautiful, and on the very last rock, a white lighthouse with a red roof.

serial-johnny-5-6.text: Darlene's brother was named Walt. He was tall and quiet and had a beard like a winter storm. He shook Gulliver's wing and said, you're late.

serial-johnny-5-7.text: I said, I'm a sailor, Walt, I'm always late. And he laughed. Just once. I found out later that's about once a month for Walt.

serial-johnny-5-8.text: The work was simple, but there was a lot of it. Gulliver cleaned the big glass lens until it sparkled.

serial-johnny-5-9.text: And he painted the spiral stairs, all one hundred and twelve of them.

serial-tokyo-1-1.text: On the last night of August, a little train pulled into Nakameguro Station, and Rosie stepped off it with two big suitcases.

serial-tokyo-1-10.text: Welcome, welcome! You must be Rosie. How was your flight? Long, I'm sure. Come in, come in. Shoes off right here, please.

serial-tokyo-1-11.text: The apartment was one room, six tatami mats, with a tiny kitchen, a tiny bathroom, and a sliding glass door to a tiny balcony.

serial-tokyo-1-12.text: Everything was small and clean, and it all fit together like a puzzle. Rosie loved it right away.

serial-tokyo-1-13.text: Now, this is very important. The trash schedule. Burnable trash on Tuesdays and Fridays. Plastic on Wednesdays. Cans and bottles every other Thursday.

serial-tokyo-1-14.text: Every other Thursday. Okay. I'm gonna need to write this down. Actually, can I just take a picture of it?

serial-tokyo-1-15.text: Of course, of course. It's a lot to take in on your first night. Don't worry. You'll get the hang of it. Everybody does.

serial-tokyo-1-16.text: He showed her how the hot water worked, which buttons on the toilet did what, and where to leave her shoes. Then he handed her the folder.

serial-tokyo-1-17.text: Make yourself at home, Rosie. And if you need anything at all, my number's on the first page. Good night!

serial-tokyo-1-18.text: And then he was gone, and it was very, very quiet.

serial-tokyo-1-19.text: Rosie sat down in the middle of her new room. There was no furniture yet. Just her suitcases, the folder, and the hum of the fridge.

serial-tokyo-1-2.text: She also had a backpack that was much too full, a map on her phone, and a key she had never used.

serial-tokyo-1-20.text: Hi, apartment. I'm Rosie. I guess we live together now. I promise I'll learn the trash schedule.

serial-tokyo-1-21.text: She opened the glass door and stepped out onto the balcony. From there, she could see a little piece of the river, and the city lights beyond it.

serial-tokyo-1-22.text: Somewhere down the street, a train went by. Somewhere else, a dog barked twice, and then thought better of it.

serial-tokyo-1-23.text: Then a door opened downstairs, and a voice called up to her, soft and friendly.

serial-tokyo-1-24.text: Hello? Are you the new neighbor? I heard the suitcases on the stairs. I'm Gayle. I live right below you.

serial-tokyo-1-25.text: Gayle was an older lady with reading glasses on a chain, and she was holding a watering can, even though it was dark.

serial-tokyo-1-26.text: Hi! Yes, I'm Rosie. I just got here. Sorry about the noise. Those suitcases weigh about as much as I do.

serial-tokyo-1-27.text: Oh, don't worry about it, dear. I lived in California for ten years when I was young. I remember my first night there.

serial-tokyo-1-28.text: Get some sleep. Tomorrow, everything will feel a little less strange. And come knock if you need anything.

serial-tokyo-1-29.text: Rosie thanked her and went back inside. She meant to unpack. She meant to take a shower. She meant to call her mom.

serial-tokyo-1-3.text: Two weeks ago, she was living in a small town in Ohio. Now she had a job in Tokyo, and an apartment of her own.

serial-tokyo-1-30.text: Instead, she lay down on the tatami for just a minute, still in her clothes, and she was out like a light.

serial-tokyo-1-31.text: It wasn't even ten o'clock. Outside, the cicadas finally stopped, and the river kept going, slow and dark, under the cherry trees.

serial-tokyo-1-4.text: It was her first time living alone. Her mom had cried at the airport. Rosie had cried a little on the plane, too.

serial-tokyo-1-5.text: The air was hot and heavy, even at nine at night. The cicadas were still buzzing in the trees, like somebody had left a radio on.

serial-tokyo-1-6.text: She rolled her suitcases along a narrow street by the Meguro River. The water was low and quiet, and cherry trees leaned over it from both sides.

serial-tokyo-1-7.text: Okay. Left at the bakery, then right at the vending machine. Wait. There's a vending machine on every corner. This could take a while.

serial-tokyo-1-8.text: Her building was small and white, just two floors, with stairs on the outside and a row of potted plants by the front door.

serial-tokyo-1-9.text: The landlord, Tom Nook, was waiting under the light with a folder, smiling like he had been waiting all day.

serial-tokyo-2-1.text: Rosie opened her eyes. The room was dark. For a moment, she had no idea where she was, or why the floor smelled like grass.

serial-tokyo-2-10.text: Rosie took her time. She picked out an egg sandwich, two rice balls, a little box of salmon and rice, and, after some thought, a pudding.

serial-tokyo-2-11.text: Want me to heat that up for ya? It only takes like a minute. And d'you need a bag? Chopsticks?

serial-tokyo-2-12.text: Yes, please. And yes to the bag, and yes to chopsticks. And no, sorry, I don't have a points card. I just got here.

serial-tokyo-2-13.text: No worries. Hey, is this your first konbini rice ball? Here, lemme show you. There's a trick to it.

serial-tokyo-2-14.text: He picked up one of the rice balls and showed her the little numbers printed on the plastic. One, two, three.

serial-tokyo-2-15.text: Pull number one, straight down the middle. Then two, then three. And that's it. The seaweed stays nice and crispy.

serial-tokyo-2-16.text: Rosie tried the second one herself. She pulled number one. Then number three. Then number two.

serial-tokyo-2-17.text: The seaweed tore in half and stayed stuck inside the plastic. The rice fell into her hand in one big lump.

serial-tokyo-2-18.text: Hey, that's okay. Ev'rybody messes it up the first time. It still tastes the same. Seriously, don't worry about it.

serial-tokyo-2-19.text: Thank you. Really. You're only the third person I've really talked to in Tokyo. Thanks, Sherb.

serial-tokyo-2-2.text: Then she remembered. Tokyo. The tatami. Her phone said it was three in the morning, and she was wide awake.

serial-tokyo-2-20.text: She ate the egg sandwich on a bench by the river. It was soft and sweet and perfect.

serial-tokyo-2-21.text: Slowly, the sky turned gray, then pink. An old man walked by with a tiny dog in a stroller. A crow said something loud from a power line.

serial-tokyo-2-22.text: And then, with no warning at all, it started to rain. Not a gentle rain. A big summer rain, warm and heavy, all at once.

serial-tokyo-2-23.text: Oh, c'mon! Seriously? It was totally clear a second ago!

serial-tokyo-2-24.text: She ran home with the plastic bag over her head. By the time she reached her street, she was soaked. Only the pudding was dry.

serial-tokyo-2-25.text: At the corner, someone was standing under a big navy umbrella with a wooden handle. It was Gayle, coming home from her morning walk.

serial-tokyo-2-26.text: Good morning, dear! My goodness, look at you. Come here, come under. The weather changes its mind fast in summer.

serial-tokyo-2-27.text: They walked home together under the big umbrella. At the front door, Gayle closed it, shook it once, and handed it to Rosie.

serial-tokyo-2-28.text: Here. Keep this for now. It's supposed to rain all week, and you start work tomorrow, don't you? I have more umbrellas than I need.

serial-tokyo-2-29.text: Are you sure? Thank you so much. I'll bring it right back, I promise. As soon as the rain stops.

serial-tokyo-2-3.text: Oh no. This is jet lag, isn't it? My body thinks it's lunchtime. And I'm starving. I haven't eaten since the plane.

serial-tokyo-2-30.text: Oh, there's no hurry. Bring it back whenever. That's what neighbors are for.

serial-tokyo-2-31.text: Upstairs, Rosie leaned the umbrella by her door, where she would see it. Then she ate the pudding, very slowly, and watched the rain.

serial-tokyo-2-32.text: She fell asleep again right there by the window, with the spoon still in her hand. This time, she slept until noon.

serial-tokyo-2-4.text: There was nothing in her kitchen but a bottle of water and some tea bags from her mom. So she put on her sneakers and went out.

serial-tokyo-2-5.text: The street was empty. But down at the corner there was a light, big and bright, like a lighthouse in the dark.

serial-tokyo-2-6.text: It was a convenience store, open all night, like they always are in Japan. The doors slid open with a little song.

serial-tokyo-2-7.text: Inside, it was cool and clean and full of everything. Rice balls. Sandwiches. Hot drinks in a warm little case. Ice cream. Socks. Even neckties.

serial-tokyo-2-8.text: Behind the counter was a sleepy young goat with a name tag that said Sherb, a college student working the night shift.

serial-tokyo-2-9.text: Oh, hey. G'morning. Or, um, g'night? Honestly, I'm not sure anymore at this hour. Take your time.

serial-tokyo-3-1.text: In Japan, when you move, you have to tell the ward office within two weeks. Rosie had a reminder on her phone, with three exclamation points.

serial-tokyo-3-10.text: The machine gave her a little paper ticket. Number forty-two. The screen above the counters said number twenty-nine.

serial-tokyo-3-11.text: Okay. Thirteen people ahead of me. That's fine. I've got a pen. I've got a form. I can do this.

serial-tokyo-3-12.text: The form had a lot of boxes. Name. Date of birth. Old address. New address. She filled them all out carefully, in her neatest handwriting.

serial-tokyo-3-13.text: When number forty-two came up, Orville was at the counter, and he seemed very happy to see her again.

serial-tokyo-3-14.text: Ah, it's you! Let me see. Very good. Very good. Oh. Oh, I see. Your address is the other way around.

serial-tokyo-3-15.text: The other way around? Whaddaya mean?

serial-tokyo-3-16.text: In America, you start small. Your apartment, your street, your city. In Japan, we start big. Tokyo first. Then the ward, the neighborhood, the block, then your building.

serial-tokyo-3-17.text: Oh, that's funny. It's like zooming in on a map instead of out. Okay, gimme one second.

serial-tokyo-3-18.text: She wrote it all again, from big to small. Orville checked every line with his finger, nodding at each one.

serial-tokyo-3-19.text: Then he printed her new address on the back of her residence card and handed it to her with both hands.

serial-tokyo-3-2.text: So on Monday morning, she took a few hours off work and walked to the ward office by the station. It was raining again.

serial-tokyo-3-20.text: Perfect. Now, one more thing. Health insurance. That's a different counter, over there on the right. Please take another number.

serial-tokyo-3-21.text: Another number? Okay. Sure. Why not.

serial-tokyo-3-22.text: The second number was fifty-eight. She sat down again. The lady next to her was knitting a tiny sweater. The man on her other side was asleep.

serial-tokyo-3-23.text: She texted Nana, her coworker at the design studio in Ebisu, who had lived in Tokyo for years. Nana sent a voice message back.

serial-tokyo-3-24.text: Oh, the ward office! I remember. Next time, bring a book. And snacks. Don't worry, it's always slow, but it always works out.

serial-tokyo-3-25.text: By the time she had her insurance card, it was almost one o'clock. It had taken all morning.

serial-tokyo-3-26.text: But walking outside with a brand new card in her bag, she felt like she had won a prize.

serial-tokyo-3-27.text: Excuse me! Rosie! Wait, please! Your umbrella! You forgot your umbrella!

serial-tokyo-3-28.text: Orville came running down the front steps, holding Gayle's big navy umbrella over his head like a flag.

serial-tokyo-3-29.text: Oh my gosh, thank you! It's not even mine. My neighbor would never forgive me. I owe you one, Orville.

serial-tokyo-3-3.text: She took Gayle's umbrella. Of course she did. It was the only umbrella she had.

serial-tokyo-3-30.text: You're welcome. And welcome to the neighborhood. Now it's official. You're on paper! Have a nice day!

serial-tokyo-3-31.text: For lunch, she found a tiny restaurant with plastic food in the window, and pointed at the grilled fish. It came with rice, soup, and pickles.

serial-tokyo-3-32.text: On the way home, the rain stopped. She went straight to Gayle's door to give back the umbrella. She knocked. Nobody answered.

serial-tokyo-3-33.text: There was only a little note on the door, in neat handwriting. Visiting my sister. Back on Saturday. Could you water my tomatoes? G.

serial-tokyo-3-34.text: So Rosie watered the tomatoes, and carried the umbrella back upstairs. And that night, she stuck ticket number forty-two on her fridge.

serial-tokyo-3-4.text: The ward office was a big, busy building, full of signs, counters, and people waiting quietly in rows of chairs.

serial-tokyo-3-5.text: Rosie stood in the middle of the lobby and turned around slowly, like someone looking for their car in a parking lot.

serial-tokyo-3-6.text: A man at the information desk waved her over. He had a neat tie, a big smile, and a name tag: Orville.

serial-tokyo-3-7.text: Good morning! Welcome! How can I help you? Please, don't be shy. I'm practicing my English. I love to practice.

serial-tokyo-3-8.text: Hi! I just moved here, and I think I need to register my address? I'm sorry, I don't really know how this works.

serial-tokyo-3-9.text: No problem at all. First, please take a number from the machine. Then fill out this form, and have a seat.

serial-tokyo-4-1.text: On Saturday afternoon, Rosie heard drums. Not far away. Close. Right outside her window.

serial-tokyo-4-10.text: Then the drums got louder, and the crowd moved to the sides of the street. Here it came.

serial-tokyo-4-11.text: It was a small golden shrine on thick wooden poles, carried on the shoulders of about thirty people, all shouting together.

serial-tokyo-4-12.text: That's the mikoshi. It's like a shrine you can carry. People say the god of the shrine rides inside and gets a tour of the neighborhood.

serial-tokyo-4-13.text: In the front, shouting louder than anyone, was a big bear in a white headband. When he saw Rosie, he grinned and waved her over.

serial-tokyo-4-14.text: Hey! You're the new girl in Mr. Nook's building, right? I'm Teddy, from the neighborhood association. C'mon, grab a pole! Give it a shot!

serial-tokyo-4-15.text: Me? Really? Are you sure? I don't know the words!

serial-tokyo-4-16.text: Easy. There's only one word. Wasshoi! You shout it, and you push. That's the whole thing. You got this!

serial-tokyo-4-17.text: So Rosie squeezed in under one of the poles, between a tall man and a tiny grandmother who was much stronger than she looked.

serial-tokyo-4-18.text: The pole was heavy on her shoulder. Everyone moved together, shouted together, and bounced the shrine up and down.

serial-tokyo-4-19.text: Wasshoi, wasshoi. She shouted until her voice cracked. She had no idea where they were going, and she didn't care.

serial-tokyo-4-2.text: She looked down from the balcony. Her quiet little street had changed. There were paper lanterns on strings, and food stands all the way to the river.

serial-tokyo-4-20.text: After two blocks, her shoulder was sore, and she was laughing so hard she could barely breathe.

serial-tokyo-4-21.text: See? Now you're part of the neighborhood. Next year, you're carrying it the whole way. No excuses!

serial-tokyo-4-22.text: Near the river was a stand with a shallow pool full of little orange goldfish. Behind it, looking sleepy, was Sherb from the convenience store.

serial-tokyo-4-23.text: Oh, hey! It's the rice ball girl! My uncle runs this stand. Wanna try? Ya get a paper scoop. If ya catch a fish, ya keep it.

serial-tokyo-4-24.text: The scoop was just a thin circle of paper on a plastic handle. Rosie leaned over and chased one little fish into a corner, very carefully.

serial-tokyo-4-25.text: She lifted it. For one second, the fish was on the scoop. Then the paper tore, and it dropped back in with a tiny splash.

serial-tokyo-4-26.text: No! I almost had it! It was right there!

serial-tokyo-4-27.text: Yeah, ev'rybody says that. Here, don't tell my uncle. You can have this one anyway. This little guy likes you. I can tell.

serial-tokyo-4-28.text: He handed her a small plastic bag of water. Inside, one little orange fish looked at her very seriously.

serial-tokyo-4-29.text: Hi, little guy. I'm gonna call you Mochi. Welcome to the family. It's just the two of us, but it's a nice apartment.

serial-tokyo-4-3.text: Her phone buzzed. It was Nana, standing in the street below and waving, in a blue cotton robe called a yukata.

serial-tokyo-4-30.text: On the way home, she ran into Gayle, back from her sister's, in a pale purple yukata.

serial-tokyo-4-31.text: Rosie held up the fish, and then she started to say sorry about the umbrella.

serial-tokyo-4-32.text: Oh, you got one! Wonderful. And thank you for watering my tomatoes. The umbrella? Hang on to it. It's going to rain tomorrow.

serial-tokyo-4-33.text: That night, Mochi swam around and around in a salad bowl on the counter. Rosie lay on the tatami, with a sore shoulder and a full stomach.

serial-tokyo-4-34.text: Through the open window, she could still hear the drums, far away now, and somebody, somewhere, still shouting wasshoi.

serial-tokyo-4-4.text: Surprise! It's the shrine festival! It's the biggest night of the year on your street. Ya gotta come down!

serial-tokyo-4-5.text: There's a festival? On my street? Nobody told me! Okay, count me in. Gimme two minutes.

serial-tokyo-4-6.text: The street smelled like grilled corn and soy sauce. Kids ran past with masks on the backs of their heads. Old men sat fanning themselves.

serial-tokyo-4-7.text: Okay, here's the plan. We eat everything. Fried noodles first. Then chocolate bananas. Then shaved ice. Trust me.

serial-tokyo-4-8.text: They ate fried noodles from paper boats, standing up, and shared a chocolate banana with rainbow sprinkles.

serial-tokyo-4-9.text: Rosie ate her strawberry shaved ice much too fast and gave herself a brain freeze.

serial-tokyo-5-1.text: The next Saturday night, Rosie was brushing her teeth when the bathroom mirror began to shake.

serial-tokyo-5-10.text: Gayle made them both cold barley tea, and they drank it on Rosie's floor until her hands stopped shaking.

serial-tokyo-5-11.text: The next morning, the school playground was full of neighbors. Kids, grandparents, families with strollers. Tom Nook was there with a clipboard, of course.

serial-tokyo-5-12.text: Good morning, everyone! Thank you for coming! Yes, yes. Please find your name on the list. And Rosie, welcome to your very first drill!

serial-tokyo-5-13.text: Firefighters had set up stations all around the playground. At one, people were taking turns with a fire extinguisher on a pretend fire.

serial-tokyo-5-14.text: At another, there was a tent full of harmless white smoke, and you walked through it bent over low, a cloth over your mouth.

serial-tokyo-5-15.text: And at the far end was a truck with a little kitchen built on the back. The sign said Earthquake Experience.

serial-tokyo-5-16.text: The firefighter in charge was a gray wolf with a serious face and a loud voice. His name, of all things, was Chief.

serial-tokyo-5-17.text: All right. In this room, we make a real earthquake. When it starts, get under the table and hold on to the leg. Don't let go. Got it?

serial-tokyo-5-18.text: Got it. Under the table. Hold on to the leg. Don't let go. Wait. How big is big?

serial-tokyo-5-19.text: Big enough. Don't worry, it's safe. It's better to feel it here, with me, than for the first time at home, alone.

serial-tokyo-5-2.text: At first, she thought it was a truck. Then the ceiling light started to swing, and the water in Mochi's bowl moved like a tiny ocean.

serial-tokyo-5-20.text: Rosie and Gayle sat down in the little kitchen. And then the whole room began to shake. Not a little. A lot. Like being inside a washing machine.

serial-tokyo-5-21.text: Rosie dove under the table and held on to the leg with both hands. Next to her, Gayle was holding on too, and somehow she was laughing.

serial-tokyo-5-22.text: Hold on tight, dear! Here comes the big part! Oh, my glasses! There they go!

serial-tokyo-5-23.text: When it stopped, Rosie crawled out. Her legs felt like noodles. Chief looked at her for a long moment. Then he gave her a thumbs-up.

serial-tokyo-5-24.text: Good. You stayed under. That's the most important thing. Now. Do you have an emergency bag at home?

serial-tokyo-5-25.text: An emergency bag? Um. I have a suitcase. And a few rice balls. Does that count?

serial-tokyo-5-26.text: Don't worry, I'll help you make one. Water, a flashlight, a radio, some crackers. You never know. Better safe than sorry.

serial-tokyo-5-27.text: That afternoon, they filled a red backpack together. Bottles of water. A flashlight. A little radio. Hard crackers that would keep for years.

serial-tokyo-5-28.text: Gayle also put in a pair of socks, a whistle, and a small bag of hard candy.

serial-tokyo-5-29.text: The candy is for your nerves. That's not official. That's just my advice.

serial-tokyo-5-3.text: Oh. Oh no. Is this an earthquake? This is an earthquake. Okay. Okay. What do I do? What do I do?

serial-tokyo-5-30.text: Back home, Rosie put the red backpack by her door, next to Gayle's navy umbrella. Looking at them, she felt a little braver.

serial-tokyo-5-31.text: Okay, Mochi. If the floor moves again, I'm gettin' under the table. And you're, well, you're already in the water. You'll be fine.

serial-tokyo-5-32.text: That night, a train went by, and the glasses rattled a little on the shelf. Rosie opened one eye. Then she smiled, and went back to sleep.

serial-tokyo-5-4.text: She stood very still, with the toothbrush in her mouth. The floor creaked. The glasses in the kitchen rattled.

serial-tokyo-5-5.text: After maybe ten seconds, it just stopped. The light swung a little more and was still. Outside, a dog barked once.

serial-tokyo-5-6.text: Her heart was pounding. Then she heard footsteps on the stairs, and a gentle knock on her door.

serial-tokyo-5-7.text: Rosie? It's Gayle. Are you all right, dear? I thought I'd better check on you. Was that your first one?

serial-tokyo-5-8.text: Yes! I just stood there. With a toothbrush. I didn't know what to do. Was that a big one?

serial-tokyo-5-9.text: Oh, no, that was a small one. We get those now and then. But there's a neighborhood drill tomorrow morning, at the school. Come with me.

serial-tokyo-6-1.text: A few days later, the evenings were finally cooler. The cicadas had gone quiet, and the crickets had taken over.

serial-tokyo-6-10.text: Rosie was nervous. But nobody was looking at anybody. Everyone was just there to get clean and warm, and to talk about their grandchildren.

serial-tokyo-6-11.text: Rule number one. You wash first, sitting on a stool. Then you get in. The bath is for soaking, not for washing.

serial-tokyo-6-12.text: So they sat on low plastic stools in front of little mirrors and washed. Then Rosie stood up, turned around, and saw the wall.

serial-tokyo-6-13.text: It was covered with a huge painting of Mount Fuji. Blue sky, snow on top, and a blue lake at the bottom.

serial-tokyo-6-14.text: Whoa. Gayle. There's a mountain. There's a whole mountain on the wall.

serial-tokyo-6-15.text: Isn't it lovely? A lot of the old bathhouses have one. Somebody painted it by hand, and every few years, they touch it up.

serial-tokyo-6-16.text: Then Rosie put one foot in the water, and pulled it right back out.

serial-tokyo-6-17.text: Oh my gosh, it's so hot! How is anybody sitting in this? Are you sure this isn't soup?

serial-tokyo-6-18.text: Take it slow. One foot, then the other. Then sit, and don't move. Believe me, in a minute, you won't wanna get out.

serial-tokyo-6-19.text: Rosie went in very slowly. Then she sat down, up to her shoulders, and let out a long breath.

serial-tokyo-6-2.text: One Thursday, Rosie came home late, stiff from a long day at her desk. Gayle was on the stairs, holding a little plastic basket.

serial-tokyo-6-20.text: The heat went into her shoulders, her back, and her tired feet. The ward office forms, the trash days, all of it just floated away.

serial-tokyo-6-21.text: Okay. I take it back. This is the best thing that's ever happened to me. I'm never gettin' out. I live here now.

serial-tokyo-6-22.text: An old lady across the bath laughed and said something to Gayle in Japanese. Gayle laughed too.

serial-tokyo-6-23.text: Wait, what'd she say? Was it about me?

serial-tokyo-6-24.text: She said you look like you've been coming here for years. That's a compliment, dear. A big one.

serial-tokyo-6-25.text: They soaked until their faces were pink. Then they got dressed, and Gayle bought two little glass bottles of coffee milk from a fridge by the door.

serial-tokyo-6-26.text: Now, this is important. You drink it standing up, with one hand on your hip. Like this. Don't ask me why. It's just how it's done.

serial-tokyo-6-27.text: So they stood side by side, each with one hand on her hip, and drank their coffee milk all at once. It was sweet and cold and perfect.

serial-tokyo-6-28.text: Oh, that hits the spot. Gayle, I'm serious. Can we do this every Thursday?

serial-tokyo-6-29.text: Every Thursday. It's a date. But next time, you bring your own towel.

serial-tokyo-6-3.text: Perfect timing! I'm going to the bathhouse. Why don't you come along? Nothing fixes a long day like a hot bath. Bring a towel.

serial-tokyo-6-30.text: Outside, it had started to drizzle. Rosie opened the big navy umbrella over both of them, and they walked home slowly, warm all the way through.

serial-tokyo-6-31.text: You know, I keep meaning to give this back to you. And then it rains every single time.

serial-tokyo-6-32.text: Then it's doing its job, isn't it? Keep it a little longer.

serial-tokyo-6-33.text: That night, Rosie slept better than ever. She dreamed she was floating on a warm blue lake, at the foot of a very big mountain.

serial-tokyo-6-4.text: A public bath? With other people? Um. I've never done that. Is it, like, ev'rybody together?

serial-tokyo-6-5.text: Men on one side, women on the other. Don't worry, I'll show you everything. And if you hate it, you never have to go again.

serial-tokyo-6-6.text: The bathhouse was three streets away, on a corner. It had a tall chimney, a blue cloth curtain over the door, and a sign Rosie couldn't read yet.

serial-tokyo-6-7.text: Inside, they put their shoes in little lockers with wooden keys, and Gayle paid for both of them before Rosie could find her wallet.

serial-tokyo-6-8.text: My treat. You're a first-timer, and first-timers don't pay. That's my rule, not theirs.

serial-tokyo-6-9.text: In the changing room, a few older ladies were drying their hair. One of them smiled at Rosie, the kind of smile that says, oh, a new one.

serial-tokyo-7-1.text: By the end of September, Rosie had been in Tokyo for almost a month. She knew, because she had been crossing off the days on her calendar.

serial-tokyo-7-10.text: Rosie bought both boxes, and just in case.

serial-tokyo-7-11.text: That evening, she knocked on Gayle's door with a box of sweets, the big navy umbrella, and a very red face.

serial-tokyo-7-12.text: Gayle, I'm so sorry. I just found out I was supposed to bring you a gift when I moved in. So, here. A month late.

serial-tokyo-7-13.text: And here's your umbrella. Finally. Thank you for lending it to me.

serial-tokyo-7-14.text: Oh, Rosie. You shouldn't have. You watered my tomatoes. You came to the bath with me. That's better than any box of sweets.

serial-tokyo-7-15.text: Gayle took the sweets. Then she looked at the umbrella for a moment, and gently pushed it back into Rosie's hands.

serial-tokyo-7-16.text: No, you keep this one. It knows the way to your door now. And any time you need a reason to knock, you'll have one.

serial-tokyo-7-17.text: Rosie didn't trust herself to say anything. So she just gave her a hug, umbrella and all.

serial-tokyo-7-18.text: Later, when it was dark, they met at the little park by the river. Tom Nook brought folding chairs. Nana brought a thermos of tea.

serial-tokyo-7-19.text: And Sherb came over on his break, still in his uniform, with a bag of snacks the store was about to throw away.

serial-tokyo-7-2.text: She knew a lot of things now. Burnable trash on Tuesdays and Fridays. Pull number one, then two, then three. Wash first, then soak.

serial-tokyo-7-20.text: What a night! Not a single cloud. Yes, yes. You know, Rosie, people here say there's a rabbit in the moon, making rice cakes. Look closely.

serial-tokyo-7-21.text: A rabbit? Really? Where? Back home, people say there's a face. The man in the moon.

serial-tokyo-7-22.text: Look at the dark parts. There are his long ears. There's his little hammer. And there, that's the bowl he makes the rice cakes in.

serial-tokyo-7-23.text: Oh! I see it! I actually see it! Now I'm never gonna be able to unsee that.

serial-tokyo-7-24.text: They ate the dumplings, which were soft and chewy and only a little bit sweet. Sherb ate four. Nobody said anything.

serial-tokyo-7-25.text: So? One month. How does it feel? Honestly.

serial-tokyo-7-26.text: Honestly? On my first night, I sat on the floor and talked to my apartment. I was so lonely.

serial-tokyo-7-27.text: And now look. I have a neighbor, and a landlord, and a coworker, and a convenience store guy.

serial-tokyo-7-28.text: Hey, I'm not just the convenience store guy. I'm also the goldfish guy.

serial-tokyo-7-29.text: And a goldfish guy. And a goldfish. And a bath on Thursdays. I think I really live here now.

serial-tokyo-7-3.text: She knew which vending machine had hot corn soup, and which bakery had melon bread at four o'clock. She didn't need the map anymore.

serial-tokyo-7-30.text: Time flies, doesn't it? You'll see. Next year, you'll be the one lending an umbrella to somebody new.

serial-tokyo-7-31.text: When the tea was gone, everybody said good night and went home, one by one, down the little streets by the river.

serial-tokyo-7-32.text: Rosie climbed the stairs, said good night to Mochi, and stood the big navy umbrella by her door. Her umbrella now.

serial-tokyo-7-33.text: Then she called her mom, who was just having breakfast back in Ohio, and told her all about the rabbit.

serial-tokyo-7-34.text: Outside, the moon was high and white over the river. And the whole neighborhood was asleep under it. Goodnight.

serial-tokyo-7-4.text: On Friday afternoon, at the studio, Nana leaned over the little wall between their desks.

serial-tokyo-7-5.text: Hey, tonight's the harvest moon. It's kinda a thing here. You look at the moon, eat little white rice dumplings, and just hang out.

serial-tokyo-7-6.text: Oh, and when you move in somewhere, you're s'posed to bring your neighbors a little gift. Like a box of sweets. Did you do that?

serial-tokyo-7-7.text: A gift? When you move in? No! Nobody told me! It's been a whole month! And Gayle has done so much for me.

serial-tokyo-7-8.text: So on the way home, Rosie stopped at the sweet shop by the station, and then at the convenience store, where Sherb was just starting his shift.

serial-tokyo-7-9.text: Moon dumplings? Yeah, we got 'em. You're lucky. Last two boxes. Are you havin' a party or somethin'?
